examples: The riser runs up through all six floors.

examples: The addition breaks up the roofline.
Every house on the block has the same roofline.
Dormers change the roofline completely.

entries.meaning: The lower edge of a roof that hangs out past the wall. ---
examples: Birds nest under the eaves.
Icicles hang from the eaves all winter.
The eaves keep rain off the siding.
entries.contrast: Nearly always used in the plural: 'under the eaves'.

entries.meaning: The finished underside of a roof overhang or an overhead structure. ---
examples: Squirrels chewed through the soffit.
Vents in the soffit let the attic breathe.
They replaced the rotted soffits.

entries.meaning: The vertical pipe that carries rainwater from the gutter to the ground. ---
examples: The downspout is clogged with leaves.
Water pooled where the downspout empties.
Both downspouts drain into the yard.
entries.contrast: American; the British say 'drainpipe'.

entries.meaning: The triangle of wall between the two slopes of a roof. ---
examples: A round window sits high in the gable.
The house has gables on three sides.
They painted the gable a darker shade.
entries.русский: щипец, треугольная часть стены под крышей

entries.meaning: A small structure with a window that sticks out from a sloping roof. ---
examples: The attic bedroom has two dormers.
A dormer would bring light into the loft.
The dormer leaks where it meets the roof.

entries.meaning: A small dome-shaped structure built on top of a roof. ---
examples: A white cupola tops the barn.
The cupola has a weather vane on it.
Cupolas were added for light and ventilation.
entries.contrast: Stress the first syllable: KYOO-puh-luh.

entries.meaning: Turret has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The old house on the corner has a round turret.
Her bedroom is inside the turret.
Stone turrets stand at each end of the castle.
The tank's turret swung slowly to the right.
A shell struck the forward turret.
The gunner sat in a glass turret under the plane.

senses.head: A small tower built onto the corner of a building
examples: The old house on the corner has a round turret.
Her bedroom is inside the turret.
Stone turrets stand at each end of the castle.

senses.head: The rotating structure on a tank, ship, or aircraft that holds a gun
examples: The tank's turret swung slowly to the right.
A shell struck the forward turret.
The gunner sat in a glass turret under the plane.

entries.meaning: A low wall along the edge of a roof, balcony, or bridge. ---
examples: He leaned over the parapet to look down at the street.
The parapet hides the rooftop equipment.
Snow drifts against the parapets.

entries.meaning: The horizontal beam across the top of a door or window opening. ---
examples: A steel lintel carries the wall above the garage door.
The stone lintel is carved with a date.
Cracked lintels let the brick above them sag.

entries.meaning: The wedge-shaped stone at the top of an arch that locks the others in place. ---
examples: The keystone is carved with a lion's head.
Pull out the keystone and the arch collapses.
Each window has a painted keystone above it.

entries.meaning: A small window above a door. ---
examples: Light comes through the transom over the front door.
Old apartments have transoms you can open for air.
Somebody painted the transom shut.

entries.meaning: A railing supported by a row of short posts along a balcony or staircase. ---
examples: A stone balustrade runs along the terrace.
The balustrade on the porch is rotting.
Marble balustrades line the grand staircase.

entries.meaning: A base that a column, statue, or sink stands on. ---
examples: The bust sits on a marble pedestal.
We put in a pedestal sink to save space.
The pedestals are all chipped at the corners.

entries.meaning: A row of evenly spaced columns supporting a roof or a line of arches. ---
examples: A colonnade runs along the front of the courthouse.
We walked the shaded colonnade.
Both colonnades frame the plaza.

entries.meaning: The decorative molding that projects along the top of a wall or building. ---
examples: A heavy stone cornice crowns the building.
Pigeons sit on the cornice all day.
The plaster cornices were restored.

entries.meaning: A band of decoration or carving running along the upper part of a wall. ---
examples: A carved frieze runs above the columns.
The frieze shows a hunting scene.
Painted friezes circle the whole room.
entries.contrast: Sounds exactly like 'freeze'.

entries.meaning: The triangular section above the columns at the front of a classical building. ---
examples: Statues fill the pediment of the museum.
A broken pediment sits over the doorway.
The pediments are pure decoration.

entries.meaning: A covered entrance with columns holding up a roof. ---
examples: Guests waited under the portico out of the rain.
A white portico marks the front entrance.
Both porticoes face the garden.

entries.meaning: A support built against a wall to keep it from leaning outward. ---
examples: Stone buttresses hold up the cathedral wall.
They added a buttress after the wall started to bow.
The flying buttresses are the most photographed part.

entries.meaning: Vault has 3 distinct senses.
examples: The vault over the nave is painted blue.
Ribbed vaults let builders span wider rooms.
Water stains run down the vault.
The bank keeps the gold in an underground vault.
The original documents are locked in the vault.
Two guards stood outside the vault all night.
She scored highest on the vault.
His second vault was nearly perfect.
The vault has always been her strongest event.

senses.head: An arched ceiling or roof made of stone or brick
examples: The vault over the nave is painted blue.
Ribbed vaults let builders span wider rooms.
Water stains run down the vault.

senses.head: A strong locked room where money or valuables are kept
examples: The bank keeps the gold in an underground vault.
The original documents are locked in the vault.
Two guards stood outside the vault all night.

senses.head: A jump over a piece of equipment in gymnastics, or the apparatus itself
examples: She scored highest on the vault.
His second vault was nearly perfect.
The vault has always been her strongest event.

entries.русский: свод (потолка); хранилище, сейфовая комната; опорный прыжок (в гимнастике)

entries.meaning: A round room or building, usually under a dome. ---
examples: The statue stands in the middle of the rotunda.
Their voices echoed in the rotunda.
Both rotundas are open to the public.

entries.meaning: Mezzanine has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The bar is up on the mezzanine.
A mezzanine office overlooks the shop floor.
Mezzanines are cheap extra square footage.
We had seats in the front of the mezzanine.
Both mezzanines were nearly full.
The mezzanine has a better view than the back of the orchestra.

senses.head: A low floor built between two main floors, often open to the space below
examples: The bar is up on the mezzanine.
A mezzanine office overlooks the shop floor.
Mezzanines are cheap extra square footage.

senses.head: The lowest balcony level of a theater, above the main floor
examples: We had seats in the front of the mezzanine.
Both mezzanines were nearly full.
The mezzanine has a better view than the back of the orchestra.

entries.contrast: American theaters say mezzanine; British ones call the same level the dress circle.

entries.meaning: A building added onto or built next to a main building. ---
examples: Classes meet in the annex behind the library.
They built an annex for the archives.
Both annexes connect by a covered walkway.
entries.contrast: The noun is AN-eks; the verb 'to annex' is uh-NEKS.

entries.meaning: A carved stone figure on a building that throws rainwater clear of the wall. ---
examples: Gargoyles stare down from the roofline.
One gargoyle lost its head in a storm.
The gargoyle over the door is a grinning dog.

entries.meaning: The long central part of a church where the congregation sits. ---
examples: Light falls across the nave in the afternoon.
The nave seats four hundred people.
Columns separate the nave from the side aisles.
entries.contrast: Sounds like 'knave', an old word for a dishonest man.

entries.meaning: A tower with several stories, each with its own upturned roof. ---
examples: A wooden pagoda stands at the top of the hill.
The garden has a small stone pagoda.
The pagodas are lit up at night.

entries.meaning: A tall four-sided stone pillar that narrows to a point at the top. ---
examples: A granite obelisk marks the grave.
The obelisk is visible from across the park.
Two obelisks flank the gate.

entries.meaning: A tall slender tower on a mosque. ---
examples: The minaret rises above the rooftops.
Four minarets stand at the corners of the courtyard.
You can see the minaret from the highway.

entries.meaning: Hard reddish-brown baked clay used for tiles, pots, and building trim. ---
examples: The roof is covered in terracotta tiles.
Terracotta fades to a soft orange over time.
The frieze is molded terracotta, not stone.
entries.contrast: Also written as two words, 'terra cotta'.

entries.meaning: Iron that has been hammered and bent into railings, gates, and other decorative pieces. ---
examples: A wrought iron fence surrounds the yard.
The balcony railing is wrought iron.
Wrought iron has to be repainted to stop the rust.
entries.contrast: 'Wrought' has a silent w and rhymes with 'thought'; 'iron' is said EYE-urn.

entries.meaning: A long roofed porch along the outside of a house. ---
examples: They sat on the veranda until it got dark.
The hotel has a veranda facing the water.
Wide verandas keep the sun off the walls.
entries.contrast: Also spelled 'verandah'; most Americans just say 'porch'.

entries.meaning: A light open building used for shelter, events, or display. ---
examples: The picnic is at the park pavilion.
Each country has its own pavilion at the fair.
The pavilions are rented by the hour.

entries.meaning: A roofed shelter for a car that is open on at least one side. ---
examples: They park under the carport.
A carport is a lot cheaper than building a garage.
The wind took the roof off both carports.

entries.meaning: A long low American house with all its rooms on one floor. ---
examples: They bought a brick ranch house from the fifties.
Ranch houses are easy to get around in.
The ranch house has an attached garage.

entries.meaning: A simple house built from stacked logs. ---
examples: We rented a log cabin in the mountains.
The log cabin has a stone fireplace.
Settlers put up log cabins in a few weeks.

entries.meaning: One of a line of identical houses joined by shared side walls. ---
examples: They live in a brick row house in Baltimore.
Row houses have no side windows.
The row house is narrow but three stories tall.
entries.contrast: American; the British say 'terraced house'.

entries.meaning: A wooden mountain house with a steep roof and wide eaves. ---
examples: We stayed in a chalet near the ski lift.
The chalet sleeps eight.
Swiss-style chalets line the road up the valley.
entries.contrast: From French: the t is silent, sha-LAY.

entries.meaning: Strips of rubber or foam fitted around doors and windows to block drafts.
examples: The weatherstripping on the back door is shot.
New weatherstripping cut our heating bill.
Weatherstripping takes ten minutes to install.
